lead: Sleep hygiene is a set of behavioral and environmental habits intended to promote healthy sleep: a regular wake time, a dark, cool, quiet bedroom, daytime light, and limited caffeine, nicotine and alcohol near bedtime.[1] In looksmaxxing and skincare communities it is treated as a free foundation habit, on the reasoning that rested people look fresher, with less puffiness around the eyes, and recover better from training.

The concept was developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.[1] Online, the wider trend has picked up the label sleepmaxxing, which Wikipedia ties to the -maxxing slang family.[1] Wikipedia's article on sleep deprivation lists puffiness around the eyes, commonly called eye bags, among its effects, and notes that sleep loss is associated with lower growth hormone and higher cortisol.[3]

Reviews describe the evidence for sleep hygiene as a stand-alone insomnia treatment as inconclusive, and a 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine analysis did not favor it as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia; combined with cognitive behavioral therapy, it has shown benefit.[1][2]

chain: Less eye puffiness and better daytime recovery
Fresher-looking face and more productive training
angle.text: People adopt sleep hygiene so they sleep longer and more reliably, which they associate with a fresher eye area and skin and with better recovery between workouts. It costs nothing, which is part of why it is called a baseline habit.

infobox: Peter Hauri, No More Sleepless Nights (1977)
Fixed wake time; dark, cool, quiet room; limit caffeine, nicotine and alcohol

paras: Typical recommendations include waking at the same time daily, aiming for roughly 7 to 8 hours, seeking bright light in the day and dim light before bed, exercising earlier in the day, avoiding caffeine, nicotine and alcohol near bedtime, avoiding worry or work in bed, and keeping the bedroom quiet, dark and cool.[1] Other common advice includes getting out of bed if sleep does not come and using the bed mainly for sleep.[1]

Appearance communities treat sleep as the base layer under skincare and training: a rested face, less puffiness and more recovery capacity. Wikipedia's sleep deprivation article lists eye bags among the effects of short sleep and links sleep loss with lower growth hormone and higher cortisol.[3] Wikipedia's sleep hygiene article does not itself discuss appearance or skin.[1]

Wikipedia traces early ideas to Paolo Mantegazza in 1864, the term to Willard Moyer in 1903, expansion by Nathaniel Kleitman in 1939, and Peter Hauri's 1977 book bringing it into sleep medicine. The 1990 International Classification of Sleep Disorders added inadequate sleep hygiene as a diagnosis, removed in the 2014 edition.[1]

Wikipedia reports stronger support for avoiding noise, alcohol before bed, mentally demanding tasks before bed and trying too hard to fall asleep; weaker or lacking support for items such as mattress comfort, removing clocks and limiting fluids; and mixed results for napping and exercise. Following several recommendations together has more support than any single item.[1]

The literature notes that studies use different sets of recommendations and that there is no evidence poor sleep hygiene causes insomnia. The 2021 AASM analysis advised against recommending sleep hygiene in place of effective treatments.[1][2]

A 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favor sleep hygiene as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia, while education combined with cognitive behavioral therapy has improved insomnia in some studies.[1][2] No studies found on sleep hygiene and facial appearance in the sources reviewed here.

name: Sleep hygiene basics

card.summary: Dark, cool, quiet, regular sleep habits; a sensible baseline, but weak evidence as a stand-alone insomnia fix.
card.note: Not favored by the AASM as stand-alone insomnia therapy.

quick.overview:
Sleep hygiene is a list of habits meant to help sleep: regular times, a dark, cool, quiet room, and limiting caffeine and alcohol late.

It is a common baseline in looksmaxxing discussion. Reviews describe the evidence for it alone as weak.
quick.mechanism: It aims to align behavior and environment with the body's sleep-wake rhythm and reduce arousal at bedtime.
quick.risks: Little direct risk is reported; the AASM analysis cautioned that relying on it alone for chronic insomnia can delay effective treatment.
